summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Vietnam and has never been criminalised in Vietnamese history. The Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 without regard to gender or sexual orientation. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, prohibited prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, and prosecutions of homosexual conduct could in rare cases be brought under those labels, but pre-colonial enforcement was inconsistent and little to no state action is recorded.

Official hostility has a documented history. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use, and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and to arrest same-sex couples. Fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013. Same-sex unions were subsequently removed from the list of forbidden acts, but they confer no legal rights; the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left such unions without legal recognition.

Legal gender recognition remains unimplemented. The 2015 Civil Code amendment, passed on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and effective from January 2017, allows people who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex, but a further implementing bill is required and the provision is not fully enforced. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which forced transgender people to travel to Thailand for the procedure. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status was expected to be discussed by the National Assembly with completion targeted for 2020, as reported in November 2018; it never materialised. The law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 has still not been implemented, and a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026.

Under the Law on Citizen Identification effective 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their ID card when undergoing gender transition but must present confirmation documents, and the legal effect of that change depends on the Gender Affirmation Law being passed first. Until then, an identity document that does not match a person's presentation is a routine feature of daily life, including at healthcare encounters.

Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds, according to a Refugee Protection Division response to information request of 30 June 2022 drawing on Freedom House material of 3 March 2021. That briefing addresses treatment by society and authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City across education, employment, housing and health care.

Amnesty International's Viet Nam 2025 report finds that LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice. The report places this alongside wider repression: vaguely worded Penal Code articles 109, 116, 117 and 331 were used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, and proposed press-law rules would require disclosure of sources. Viet Nam was re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a term running until 2028.

Conversion practices have been prohibited since 3 August 2022 under Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC from the Ministry of Health, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment"; the dispatch also mandated enhanced communication in medical facilities nationwide and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. The Health Ministry had already declared in August 2022 that same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders. A Lighthouse Vietnam study published in October 2024, "Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam", nonetheless documents experiences and forms of conversion efforts in the Vietnamese context and sets out data needs.

Healthcare access is uneven in practice. A UN Viet Nam feature of 30 November 2024 reports that transgender women face routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, including staff asking "Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?", heightened scrutiny, and economic and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, with the risk concentrated among trans women in northern provinces and ethnic minorities; the feature frames accessible legal recognition as the remedy. Saigoneer reported in June 2023 that implementing guidance following the November 2015 milestone, which allowed people who changed gender to apply for a civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, stalled, leaving policy gaps; four trans Vietnamese described respectful healthcare providers whose cooperation was undone by administrative red tape.

Public assembly space narrowed in 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other Pride events during 2025. Patricia Gossman, Asia director of Human Rights Watch, described this as worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, set against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation.

Two institutional gaps are documented without an enacted outcome. In January 2015 the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute proposed to the Ministry of Public Security that homosexual and transgender prisoners be housed separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails; it stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, so no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity existed, and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented. Separately, there is no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly in Vietnam, though under government surveillance.
tangentialFactors:
Pride events expanded for more than a decade before the 2025 cancellations. Vietnam's first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012; by 2017 pride events were held in around 34 other cities and provinces, with over 35 similar events annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ. Hanoi Pride ran for a fifth consecutive year from 18 to 24 September 2017 drawing thousands, against about a hundred at the first parade, and its sixth edition in November 2018 saw more than 1,000 participants cycling to campaign for transgender rights and same-sex marriage. Several events were aired on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9.

Media framing has shifted over time. In 2002 publications such as Thế Giới Phụ Nữ and Tiếp thị & Gia đình described homosexuality as a disease and "deviant behavior"; in September 2010 Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to agree that "homosexuality is normal". The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was published on YouTube because Vietnamese broadcasters were reluctant to air it.

Public opinion measured in 2023 by Pew shows support for same-sex marriage highest among 18 to 34-year-olds at 79%, against 57% for those aged 35 and above. An earlier 2007 poll of 300 junior-high and high-school pupils at Ho Chi Minh City Pedagogical University found 80% answered "no" to the question "Is homosexuality bad?".
localsOnly:
Discrimination against LGBTIQ students is documented in domestic survey data. A 2015 study found around 44% of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14 to 22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities. A 2014 USAID report showed 54% of LGBT students said their school was not safe, with many dropping out; of those who experienced violence, one third thought about committing suicide and half of those attempted it. 85% of transgender students said they dropped out because of assault and bullying. A 2015 UNESCO study found 19% of students perceived bullying against LGBT students as "harmless", and 70% of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, with some believing conversion therapy could "cure" LGBT children.

In 2006 the government enacted legislation protecting citizens infected with HIV and people living with AIDS from discrimination, and health care is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens. The 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch mandated enhanced public communication and dissemination among medical facilities nationwide so that staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly in Vietnam, though under government surveillance.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Gender Affirmation Law will be passed, and on what terms, is unresolved in these sources; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026, seven years after completion was targeted for 2020. Until it is enacted, the practical effect of the Law on Citizen Identification provisions for transgender citizens is not sourced here.

The January 2015 proposal to house homosexual and transgender prisoners separately has no documented enacted outcome. Whether any subsequent policy on prison housing by gender identity exists is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator and a comparison to Vietnam's general homicide rate appears in this inventory, so no trans-specific killing rate can be stated. The UN feature of 30 November 2024 describes economic and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence for trans women without quantifying it.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers, including document-marker flagging or secondary screening triggered by gender presentation, is not addressed by any source in this inventory. Nothing here should be read as evidence that such screening does or does not occur.

Enforcement of the 3 August 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch is not documented; the October 2024 Lighthouse Vietnam study records conversion efforts still experienced by LGBTIQ people, but does not establish whether any were carried out by regulated medical practitioners after the ban.
